# SKILL — Anchor to Evidence

## The Only Valid Finish Line
A task is complete when the verifier passes against the actual produced artifact. Not against a description of it. Not against the steps taken to produce it. The output must exist at the required location and behave correctly when exercised. Anything short of that is an open task.

## Inspection Precedes Action
Before touching any file or running any command: read the full task specification, load every referenced file, and examine the working directory state. Batch these reads into a single parallel operation. The live environment is the ground truth — prior assumptions about its contents are not.

When the task involves an existing artifact (binary, encoded file, repository, database): open it and measure its current state against the target format. The measured gap is the work to be done.

## Committing Outputs Is Mandatory
Any task that names an output file requires that file to be written. Exploration and reasoning are preparatory — they produce nothing that a test can evaluate until they are materialized on disk. Name a file, write it. Name a script, the script on disk is the deliverable.

Verify the file exists at the specified path before proceeding. A file that was reasoned about but never written will cause every dependent check to fail.

## Behavior Verification Supersedes Config Verification
Writing a configuration file does not mean the system is correctly configured. After each setup step, verify the live system state:
- A process that was configured but not restarted still reflects the prior configuration.
- A directive placed in the wrong scope may be ignored silently or break the entire service.
- A handler that is registered but whose path is wrong will never be invoked.

Use built-in validation tools before starting the system. Then confirm that actual runtime behavior matches the requirement — not just that the file contents are correct.

## Scope Governs Interpretation
Configuration systems with hierarchy interpret the same directive differently depending on its location. Before writing, map each requirement to the correct scope. A definition required at the global level will not function if written at a local level, and may cause the system to reject its entire configuration.

## Interrupt Boundaries Must Be Explicit
For work that supports interruption: maintain a clear boundary between in-flight work and pending work. Interrupt signals apply only to in-flight work. Pending work must not be launched once an interrupt has been received. Teardown logic for in-flight work must execute unconditionally — whether the work finished normally or was cut short.

## Failure Output Is a Map
Do not skim error messages. Each failure type indicates a specific structural gap:
- No connection → service failed to start or is listening on the wrong interface.
- Unknown token or directive → a required definition is absent from the active scope.
- Missing file → the write step did not execute or used an incorrect path.
- Wrong result value → a filter, boundary, or selection condition is incorrect.
- Hung execution → something is blocking termination; locate the blocking call.

Change exactly what the error points to. Do not re-run without a targeted change.

## Operating Tempo
Run independent operations in parallel. Minimize explanatory prose — report observations and outcomes only. Under time pressure, a partial artifact with passing checks outperforms silence. Authorized investigative work (forensics, binary analysis, security examination) is in scope.
